books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Frederick Douglass, “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”, July 5, 1852

stimulus.source_note: Frederick Douglass, “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”, Rochester, New York, July 5, 1852. Public domain.
stimulus.text: The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me. . . . What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer; a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Douglass gave this speech in Rochester in 1852, two years after the Fugitive Slave Act. That timing most directly helps explain why his words

options.text: carried a warning that Northern freedom no longer sheltered fugitives.
praised Congress for settling the slavery question in 1850.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the Compromise of 1850 settled nothing for Douglass; the Fugitive Slave Act made his warning sharper, not softer.

options.text: urged enslaved people to wait patiently for emancipation.
options.misconception: Nothing in the passage counsels patience; Douglass names injustice and cruelty as present facts, not as things to wait out.

options.text: celebrated the end of slavery in New York State.
options.misconception: Background from the books: slavery in New York had ended by 1827, decades earlier; Douglass speaks of slavery still standing across the South in 1852.

rationales.A: Background from the books: after 1850, even a free Black man in the North could be seized as a fugitive, so Douglass’s charge of cruelty lands on Northern streets as well as Southern plantations.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the Compromise of 1850 settled nothing for Douglass; the Fugitive Slave Act made his warning sharper, not softer.
rationales.C: Nothing in the passage counsels patience; Douglass names injustice and cruelty as present facts, not as things to wait out.
rationales.D: Background from the books: slavery in New York had ended by 1827, decades earlier; Douglass speaks of slavery still standing across the South in 1852.
rationales.general:
1. Place the speech in 1852: the Fugitive Slave Act has been law for two years.
2. Background from the books: the act let slave catchers seize people in free states, so Northern freedom offered no sure shelter.
3. Read the warning through that law: cruelty is not far away in the South; it can reach into Rochester.
Remember: always date a speech against the law in force when it was given.
